Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Molecular Surveillance and Evolutionary Characterization of Orthohantavirus jejuense in the Republic of Korea, 2019–2025
papers.abstract: Jeju virus (JJUV), a shrew-borne member of Orthohantavirus jejuense, has been detected in geographically separated populations of Crocidura shantungensis in the Republic of Korea (ROK). However, its distribution and evolutionary characteristics remain incompletely defined. From 2019 to 2025, 56 C. shantungensis were collected from 20 sites across the ROK and screened for JJUV RNA. Viral genomic sequences were characterized using next-generation and Sanger sequencing, followed by phylogenetic, evolutionary, selection-pressure, and in silico B-cell epitope analyses. JJUV RNA was detected in 7 of 56 shrews (12.5%) from Gwangju Metropolitan City, Cheorwon, Chuncheon, and Seogwipo. Coding-complete sequences of all three genomic segments were obtained from three variants, including two from Gwangju, providing genome-resolved evidence of JJUV circulation in the southern mainland. Phylogenetic analyses revealed clear geographic clustering of O. jejuense variants from the northern mainland, Gwangju, Jeju Island, and Ulleung Island. Estimated evolutionary rates ranged from 3.53 × 10−4 to 13.49 × 10−4 substitutions/site/year. Low ratios of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rates across the nucleocapsid protein, glycoproteins Gn and Gc, and RNA-dependent RNA polymerase indicated predominantly purifying selection. Sequence- and structure-based analyses predicted six conserved linear B-cell epitope candidates across O. jejuense. Among these, Y165–K175 in the nucleocapsid protein showed the strongest combined structural support. These findings expand the known geographic and genomic diversity of O. jejuense and provide a framework for continued surveillance and future serological studies of its potential zoonotic relevance.

papers.title: ‘Desperate rodents’ pose hantavirus risk to humans — boosted by climate change and deforestation

source_records.title: ‘Desperate rodents’ pose hantavirus risk to humans — boosted by climate change and deforestation
‘Desperate rodents’ pose hantavirus risk to humans — boosted by climate change and deforestation

papers.full_text: nature health News ‘Desperate rodents’ pose hantavirus risk to humans — boosted by climate change and deforestation Rapid urbanization and changes in rodent behaviour increase the risk of human disease outbreaks, especially in Africa, but experts fear surveillance gaps leave most zoonotic infections undetected. By Tsitsi Bhobo W hen the Andes hantavirus cir­ culated on the M/V Hondius cruise ship, South Africa’s specialist hospitals quickly admitted infected patients and sequenced the virus. But infectious dis­ ease scientists warn that locally derived hanta­ virus strains — including the lethal Sangassou virus — are circulating undetected, hosted by native shrews, rodents and bats1. “At the moment, we believe that hanta­ virus probably is more prevalent [and] widespread than diagnosed in Africa,” says Tulio de Oliveira, Professor at Stellenbosch University, South Africa, and director of the Centre for Epidemic Response and Innova­ tion. Such infections are mainly “self-limited transmission clusters between rodents, other animals and humans,” he tells Nature Health. De Oliveira’s lab is one of a small number across Africa that test for viruses in wild animals, including rodents, bats and non- human primates. Surveillance gap Hantaviruses pose a bigger systematic dan­ ger to Africa’s public health architecture than previously thought, argued de Oliveira and colleagues in a recent article. Limited diag­ nostic and testing capacity and lack of moni­ toring infrastructure, combined with climate change and urbanization, are leading to more zoonotic outbreaks. Africa has a clinical surveillance gap, with viral spillovers probably occurring without being detected by stretched public health authorities. During the current Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, many of the early infections were suspected to be cases of malaria, leading to delays in the public health response. The DRC has the second highest bur­ den of malaria in the world, leading to tens of thousands of deaths each year. Many other zoonotic infections could be missed. Hillary Young, an ecologist at the University of California Santa Barbara, USA, notes that “we don’t know how big the burden of hanta­ virus is because we haven’t looked for it, really. We don’t have that surveillance.” “One of the acute problems facing Africa is that there is little clinical research into the ecology of hantaviruses, [such as] which specific animals host them,” she says. Such research, including genetics, would “empower scientists to map the interaction between hosts and viruses and calculate the possible harm to humans — in real time,” she adds. With surveillance capacity absent, doctors often report possible hantavirus infections as ‘fever of unknown origin’. “It’s hard, because hantavirus is another one of these diseases that kind of overlaps with lots of other unex­ plained febrile diseases,” says Young. This challenge persists despite South Africa having amongst the best infectious disease genomic surveillance infrastructure in the world. Laboratories across Africa are usually focused on supporting clinical studies in humans, but during outbreaks, resources are diverted to test animals for zoonotic infec­ tions. There are only a small number of such labs across the continent, such as the South Africa National Institute for Communicable Diseases, the Institut Pasteur de Dakar in Senegal and the Uganda Virus Research Unit. These labs act very quickly to develop reagents for new pathogens, test samples and develop metagenomics assays, but the bottleneck leads to inevitable delays, with zoonotic out­ breaks often underdiagnosed for weeks. Urbanization and deforestation Hantavirus spillover in Africa is likely to be linked to loss of biodiversity, rapid urbaniza­ tion and climate change. A recent outbreak of hantaviruses in South America spread beyond rural settings and into urban environments, Hantavirus particles under an electron microscope, with colour enhanced. CREDIT: ALFRED PASIEKA/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/GETTY nature health News possibly because climate variations are lead­ ing to milder and shorter winters in Argentina. Rapid urbanization — widespread across the continent — leads to increased risk, as rats breed in cities where residents regularly interact with wildlife. “We’ll have a bigger pro­ liferation of concentrated rodents,” in Africa’s fast-urbanizing landscapes, says Young, lead­ ing to more zoonotic outbreaks. Young’s research has shown how declines in large wildlife in East Africa were associated with an increase in the prevalence of a rodent- borne bacterium, Bartonella, which can infect humans — providing a link between biodiver­ sity loss and zoonotic disease outbreaks2. Climate change and change of land use in Africa drive rodents to find new breeding zones in human landscapes, warns Young. Rapid expansion of cities across Africa, many without investment in sewerage, creates food and opportunities for rodent species that are already adapted to live alongside humans. This creates the conditions for ‘boom dynamics’, says Young, where rodent popula­ tions increase rapidly. This means periods of explosive, exponential growth for rat popula­ tions followed by often calamitous declines3. “You might get really desperate rodents,” she says, where the animals are “forced into kind of aggressive behaviour. Fighting in rodents can help spread disease among them at higher prevalence.” One Health The genomic surveillance labs in Africa, Latin America and Asia have considerable expertise but fewer resources than their counterparts in high-income countries, says Young. Despite these constraints, they are doing valuable work closest to the regions where zoonotic diseases are most likely to spring up. Africa is taking a lead in shifting the ‘One Health’ model towards building long-term skills, surveillance and diagnostics infrastructure in the global south, the type of capacity that remains resilient through crises. Several African countries, including the DRC and Uganda, have adopted ‘One Health’ frame­ works, an approach pioneered by Rwanda4. But such frameworks need to extend beyond the countryside and integrate with cities in Africa, rather than thinking of these urban spaces as separated from wild rural environ­ ments, says Young. De Oliveira stresses that, although hanta­ viruses are unlikely to cause large human outbreaks — because of the biology of the virus — funding cuts for global health pose challenges. There is now a “big lack of global health funding,” he says, with the US and many Euro­ pean countries “running out of money for global health because of other priorities such as defence”. USA https://doi.org/ 10.1073/pnas.1404958111 (2014). 3. Doebeli, M., Jaque, E. C. & Ispolatov, Y. Commun. Biol. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-021-02021-4 (2021). 4. Henley, P. & Shyaka, A. Nat. Med. https://doi.org/10.1038/ s41591-024-03473-x (2025).

Fighting in rodents can help spread disease among them at higher prevalence.” One Health The genomic surveillance labs in Africa, Latin America and Asia have considerable expertise but fewer resources than their counterparts in high-income countries, says Young. Despite these constraints, they are doing valuable work closest to the regions where zoonotic diseases are most likely to spring up. Africa is taking a lead in shifting the ‘One Health’ model towards building long-term skills, surveillance and diagnostics infrastructure in the global south, the type of capacity that remains resilient through crises. Several African countries, including the DRC and Uganda, have adopted ‘One Health’ frame­ works, an approach pioneered by Rwanda4. But such frameworks need to extend beyond the countryside and integrate with cities in Africa, rather than thinking of these urban spaces as separated from wild rural environ­ ments, says Young. De Oliveira stresses that, although hanta­ viruses are unlikely to cause large human outbreaks — because of the biology of the virus — funding cuts for global health pose challenges. There is now a “big lack of global health funding,” he says, with the US and many Euro­ pean countries “running out of money for global health because of other priorities such as defence”. papers.title: Hantavirus: biology, immune responses, and pathogenesis
papers.abstract: Abstract The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise has raised global public health alarms due to its dangerous ability to person-to-person spread. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. Two principal mechanisms, virus-mediated cytopathy and host-driven immunopathology, have been proposed to account for the pathological progression, while their interplay is yet to be fully explored. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease.

analysis.background: The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise raised global public‑health alarms due to its dangerous ability to spread person‑to‑person (A1).
analysis.methods: This article is a narrative review synthesizing existing literature; specific study design, sample collection, or analytical methods are not reported in the supplied evidence (not reported in the supplied evidence).
analysis.results: The review highlights two principal pathogenic mechanisms—virus‑mediated cytopathy and host‑driven immunopathology (A3)—and emphasizes viral immune evasion coupled with uncontrolled host immune responses as core drivers (A4); hantaviruses antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy to delay early innate activation (A5); excessive CD8⁺ T‑cell and NK‑cell activation with impaired regulatory T‑cells and dysregulated humoral immunity disrupt endothelial barriers and cause organ vasculopathy (A6).
analysis.contribution: By summarizing recent research on hantavirus biology, entry, epidemiology, and immune evasion, the review informs surveillance, therapeutic development, and future research directions (A4, A7, A8).
analysis.limitations: Only abstract and partial/full text were provided; the article presents no original experimental data and does not detail its literature‑search methodology (not reported in the supplied evidence).

analysis.summary_en: Background: The recent Andes virus outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise raised global public‑health alarms due to its dangerous person‑to‑person spread (A1). Methods: This is a narrative review; specific methods are not reported (not reported in the supplied evidence). Results: Two pathogenic mechanisms—virus‑mediated cytopathy and host‑driven immunopathology—are highlighted (A3), with viral immune evasion and uncontrolled host responses identified as core drivers (A4); hantaviruses block type I interferon and autophagy (A5), and overactive CD8⁺ T cells, NK cells, and impaired regulatory/humoral immunity damage endothelial barriers (A6). Contribution: The synthesis advances understanding of hantavirus biology, informs surveillance, therapeutics, and future research (A4, A7, A8). Limitations: Only abstract and partial/full text are available; no original data or detailed search methods are reported (not reported in the supplied evidence).

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒:生物学、免疫应答与发病机制

analysis_zh.background: 最近在 MV Hondius 巡航船上发生的 安第斯病毒(ANDV)疫情因其危险的人人传人能力(A1)而引发全球公共卫生警报。
analysis_zh.methods: 本文为综述性叙述性评论,综合现有文献;所提供证据中未报告具体的研究设计、样本采集或分析方法(未在所提供证据中报告)。
analysis_zh.results: 综述指出两大主要致病机制——病毒介导的细胞病变和宿主驱动的免疫病理(A3)——并强调病毒免疫逃逸与失控的宿主免疫反应共同构成核心驱动因素(A4);汉坦病毒es 抑制I型干扰素信号通路和自噬,以延迟早期先天免疫激活(A5);过度的 CD8+ T 细胞和 NK 细胞活化、调节性 T 细胞功能受损以及体液免疫失调破坏内皮屏障,导致器官血管病变(A6)。

papers.title: Angiopoietin-1/Tie2 Activation as a Therapeutic Hypothesis for Hantavirus-Induced Vascular Permeability
papers.abstract: Severe hantavirus infection produces extensive vascular leakage, driven by a combination of endothelial dysfunction, dysregulated inflammation, VEGF-mediated hyperpermeability, angiopoietin imbalance, and degradation of the endothelial glycocalyx. This narrative review draws on the peer-reviewed literature, with particular attention to work published between 2016 and 2026, to examine how hantavirus-induced vascular permeability arises in hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), and how Angiopoietin-1 (Ang-1)/Tie2 signaling and glycocalyx injury contribute to endothelial barrier failure. Direct hantavirus evidence shows that Ang-1 inhibits hantavirus-directed endothelial permeability in vitro and that angiopoietin dysregulation tracks with disease severity in patients; findings that Tie2 activation curbs vascular leakage in sepsis and other non-hantavirus models are mechanistically suggestive but remain inferential rather than hantavirus-specific. No hantavirus animal model or clinical trial has yet evaluated Ang-1/Tie2-directed therapy, so this review treats the approach as a testable hypothesis rather than an established or recommended treatment; confirming its therapeutic value will require dedicated hantavirus-specific animal and clinical studies.

analysis.background: Severe hantavirus infection causes extensive vascular leakage through endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, VEGF, angiopoietin imbalance, and glycocalyx degradation (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The narrative review surveys literature (2016‑2026) on how hantavirus‑induced permeability arises in HFRS and HPS and the roles of Ang‑1/Tie2 signaling and glycocalyx injury (A2).
analysis.current_state: In vitro data show Ang‑1 suppresses hantavirus‑driven endothelial permeability, and patient studies link angiopoietin dysregulation with disease severity (A3).
analysis.gaps: Evidence that Tie2 activation reduces leakage comes from sepsis and other models and remains inferential for hantavirus, lacking direct hantavirus‑specific validation (A4).
analysis.future_research: Dedicated hantavirus animal models and clinical trials are needed to test Ang‑1/Tie2‑targeted therapies (A5).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Severe hantavirus infection triggers vascular leakage via multiple endothelial pathways (A1). Main directions: The review examines mechanisms of permeability in HFRS/HPS and the contribution of Ang‑1/Tie2 and glycocalyx injury (A2). Current state: Ang‑1 reduces hantavirus‑induced permeability in vitro and angiopoietin imbalance correlates with severity (A3). Gaps: Tie2 activation benefits are inferred from non‑hantavirus models, not directly proven (A4). Future research: Hantavirus‑specific animal studies and clinical trials are required to evaluate Ang‑1/Tie2 therapy (A5).

papers.title_zh: Ang-1/Tie2 激活作为 汉坦病毒 引起的血管通透性的治疗假设

analysis_zh.background: 严重的汉坦病毒感染通过内皮功能障碍、炎症、血管内皮生长因子(VEGF)、血管生成素失衡以及糖萼降解导致广泛的血管渗漏 (A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本叙述性综述检索了2016‐2026年的文献,探讨汉坦病毒诱导的通透性在肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒肺综合征中的产生机制,以及Ang‐1/Tie2信号通路和糖萼损伤的作用 (A2)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 体外实验数据显示,Ang‐1抑制汉坦病毒介导的内皮通透性,患者研究则将血管生成素失调与疾病严重程度相关联 (A3)。
analysis_zh.gaps: Tie2激活可降低渗漏的证据来源于败血症及其他模型,但对汉坦病毒仍属推断性,缺乏直接针对汉坦病毒的验证 (A4)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要专门的汉坦病毒动物模型和临床试验来检验针对Ang‐1/Tie2的治疗方案 (A5)。

papers.summary_zh: 背景:严重的汉坦病毒感染通过内皮功能障碍、炎症、血管内皮生长因子(VEGF)、血管生成素失衡以及糖萼... 主要方向:本叙述性综述检索了2016‐2026年的文献,探讨汉坦病毒诱导的通透性在肾综合征出血热和汉坦病... 研究现状:体外实验数据显示,Ang‐1抑制汉坦病毒介导的内皮通透性,患者研究则将血管生成素失调与疾病严重... 不足:Tie2激活可降低渗漏的证据来源于败血症及其他模型,但对汉坦病毒仍属推断性,缺乏直接针对汉坦病... 后续研究:需要专门的汉坦病毒动物模型和临床试验来检验针对Ang‐1/Tie2的治疗方案 (A5)。

papers.title: Large language models for hantavirus-related infectious disease risk communication during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak: an expert-rated comparative content analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for health information, but their reliability in outbreak-related public health communication remains uncertain. Hantavirus communication is challenging because messages must balance avoidance of unnecessary alarm with prevention of false reassurance, particularly during the 2026 Andes virus outbreak. This comparative, cross-sectional, expert-rated content analysis evaluated responses generated by three non-Pro publicly accessible LLMs - ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude - to 150 predefined hantavirus-related questions. Questions covered official health authority/guideline-based information, expert/clinical practice issues and public frequently asked questions. Each question was submitted using a standard zero-shot prompt and a public health risk communication prompt, generating 900 responses. Three independent experts assessed accuracy, completeness, consistency, safety and actionability using a predefined rubric. Ratings were summarised descriptively, and inter-rater reliability was assessed using percentage agreement and Fleiss’ kappa. Overall, 568 of 900 responses (63.1%) were rated as completely correct and sufficient, 232 (25.8%) as mostly correct but incomplete, and 100 (11.1%) as partially correct or potentially misleading. No response was rated as completely incorrect or overtly harmful. Within this dataset, ChatGPT had numerically the highest proportion of completely correct responses (198/300, 66.0%) and the lowest proportion of misleading responses (28/300, 9.3%); however, these differences were interpreted descriptively rather than as evidence of model superiority. Gemini and Claude had completely correct response rates of 62.7% and 60.7%, respectively. In this dataset, the generic public health risk communication prompt did not change the aggregate expert-rated categorical distribution. Major publicly accessible LLMs generated a high proportion of correct or mostly correct hantavirus risk communication responses, but approximately one in nine responses was potentially misleading. These tools may support infectious disease and outbreak-related risk communication but should not be used as stand-alone sources for clinically complex or rapidly evolving guidance without expert oversight and official-source grounding. Not applicable.

papers.title: Hantavirus mutagenesis is impacted by mutagens and host antiviral proteins
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that infect humans with high fatality rates. We currently have a poor understanding of the processes that contribute to hantavirus mutagenesis and therefore the potential for viral adaptation. To understand the drivers of mutations in hantaviruses, we calculated and compared mutational spectra across 14 divergent hantavirus species. We found that mutagens that are conserved across host species have a major impact on hantaviruses mutagenesis, contributing to at least six of the 12 possible mutation types. We found differences in mutational signatures across hantaviruses, some of which may be due to variation in host mutagen levels that are known to influence somatic mutations. However, we could find no evidence for differential mutational signatures between viruses associated with distinct diseases in humans and no evidence of tissue tropism differences between reservoir hosts. Using a novel method to quantify the impact of ZAP-mediated selection, we found that ZAP greatly influences mutational patterns in transition mutation types across hantaviruses. We also find evidence that APOBEC family proteins drive mutagenesis in all hantaviruses, with the likely exception of Nova virus. Our results therefore provide strong support that mutagens and host antiviral proteins are major contributors to hantavirus mutagenesis, thereby generating the genetic diversity necessary for viral adaptation.

Andres Floto1,3,5 2 3 Affiliations 4 1Victor Phillip Dahdaleh Heart and Lung Research Institute, Department of Medicine, 5 University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 6 2Department of Veterinary Medicine, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 7 3Cambridge Centre for AI in Medicine, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 8 4Biological and Chemical Research Centre, University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Poland 9 5Department of Medicine, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 10 *Correspondence to: Christopher Ruis (cr628@cam.ac.uk) 11 Abstract 12 Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that infect humans with high fatality rates. We 13 currently have a poor understanding of the processes that contribute to hantavirus 14 mutagenesis and therefore the potential for viral adaptation. To understand the drivers of 15 mutations in hantaviruses, we calculated and compared mutational spectra across 14 16 divergent hantavirus species. We found that mutagens that are conserved across host species 17 have a major impact on hantaviruses mutagenesis, contributing to at least six of the 12 18 possible mutation types. We found differences in mutational signatures across hantaviruses, 19 some of which may be due to variation in host mutagen levels that are known to influence 20 somatic mutations. However, we could find no evidence for differential mutational signatures 21 between viruses associated with distinct diseases in humans and no evidence of tissue 22 tropism differences between reservoir hosts. Using a novel method to quantify the impact of 23 ZAP-mediated selection, we found that ZAP greatly influences mutational patterns in transition 24 mutation types across hantaviruses. We also find evidence that APOBEC family proteins drive 25 mutagenesis in all hantaviruses, with the likely exception of Nova virus. Our results therefore 26 provide strong support that mutagens and host antiviral proteins are major contributors to 27 hantavirus mutagenesis, thereby generating the genetic diversity necessary for viral 28 adaptation. 29 Introduction 30 Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that naturally infect hosts within the orders 31 Rodentia, Eulipotyphla and Chiroptera [1–3]. Each hantavirus typically exhibits a close 32 association with one or a small number of host species within which it establishes 33 predominantly asymptomatic infections [3]. For example, Hantaan virus lives within the striped 34 field mouse (Apodemus agrarius), while Andes virus is carried by the long-tailed pygmy rice 35 rat (Oligozomys longicaudatus) [2, 4]. This host association results in most hantaviruses 36 exhibiting strong geographical restriction, determined by the range of their host [1, 3]. The 37 exception is Seoul virus which infects black rats (Rattus rattus) and brown rats (Rattus 38 norvegicus) and correspondingly exhibits a global distribution concomitant with that of its hosts 39 [2]. 40 41 Hantaviruses are capable of infecting multiple cell types, including endothelial cells, epithelial 42 cells, macrophages, follicular dendritic cells and lymphocytes and can be detected in multiple 43 tissues within their reservoir hosts including the lungs and kidneys [3, 5]. Within humans, 44 hantaviruses can cause two distinct diseases, which are associated with different viruses and 45 therefore geographical regions [1, 3, 6, 7]. Human hantavirus cases in Eurasia are associated 46 with Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), while those in the Americas are 47 associated with Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS; also called Hantavirus 48 Cardiopulmonary Syndrome or HCPS) [6, 7]. 49 50 Human hantavirus infections predominantly occur through inhalation of secretions from the 51 major host species, including faeces, saliva and urine [6, 7]. More rarely, infections can occur 52 through bites [6]. Andes virus is currently the only hantavirus with documented human-to- 53 human transmission; such events are associated with close contact and can lead to small 54 clusters of cases [8, 9]. However, zoonotic transmission events are frequent enough to lead 55 to an estimated 10,000 to 100,000 human hantavirus cases each year with an estimated 56 fatality rate of <1% to 40% depending on the virus and outbreak [6]. 57 58 Hantaviruses are within the genus Orthohantavirus and the Bunyaviridae family and as such 59 have a negative sense single stranded RNA genome [10, 11]. The genome is organised into 60 three segments, termed large (L), medium (M) and small (S), of which the M segment encodes 61 the viral glycoproteins Gn and Gc [10]. The substitution rate of hantaviruses is estimated to be 62 in the range of 10-4 to 10-2 substitutions/site/year, typical of RNA viruses [12]. This high 63 substitution rate suggests that hantaviruses are capable of rapid adaptation. 64 65 Adaptation relies on the generation of diversity and therefore on mutagenesis. To understand 66 microbial adaptation, we therefore need an understanding of the mutational processes that 67 contribute to mutagenesis. However, we currently have a poor understanding of these factors 68 within hantaviruses and therefore the processes that may assist or constrain hantavirus 69 adaptation. We and others have recently demonstrated that mutational signatures (context- 70 specific patterns of nucleotide substitution initially applied to detect the drivers of 71 tumourigenesis [13–16]) can identify active mutational processes in microbes [17–26]. We 72 have applied these methods to identify both intrinsic mutational processes encoded by the 73 microbe and extrinsic lifestyle-associated mutagen exposures [18–20, 22]. In this study, we 74 examine and compare mutational patterns across hantaviruses to identify mutational 75 processes that may contribute to hantavirus adaptation. 76 Results 77 78 Mutagens impact hantavirus mutagenesis 79 We calculated single base substitution (SBS) mutational spectra for 14 hantavirus species that 80 exhibit at least 600 sampled mutations [27] amongst M segment genetic sequences (Figure 81 1, Table S1, see Methods). We additionally carried out “tree rescaling” of each spectrum by 82 sequence composition across the respective phylogenetic tree [22]. The overall mutational 83 spectrum is highly similar across viruses at the overall level (median cosine similarity 0.978; 84 Figure S1), supporting conservation of most mutational processes. We found that, as 85 expected, each spectrum is dominated by transition mutations (median 76.7% unscaled, 86 78.1% tree rescaled; Figures 1, S2). In contrast to SARS-CoV-2 [19, 26] and influenza A virus 87 [22], T>A and A>T are typically the most common transversion mutations by raw count (Figure 88 S2). However, following tree rescaling, G>T mutations occur at a similar rate to T>A and A>T 89 mutations (Figure S2). 90 91 92 Figure 1. Mutagens influence hantavirus mutagenesis. (A) Cladogram of the evolutionary 93 relationships between the 14 analysed hantaviruses. The heatmap shows the respective host 94 family, host order, associated human disease (where known) and geographical distribution of 95 each virus. Tip labels include the virus name and, in parentheses, the common English name 96 and scientific name of the respective predominant host species. (B) The SBS mutational 97 spectrum of Seoul virus is shown as proportions of raw mutation counts (left hand panel) and 98 as the proportion of mutations within the tree rescaled spectrum (right hand panel). Asterisks 99 in the right hand panel show C>T and G>A mutations that remove ZAP-associated CG 100 contexts. (C) Comparison of symmetric mutation types in tree rescaled mutational spectra. * 101 shows randomisation P < 0.05, supporting a significant difference from a ratio of one and 102 therefore an elevation of one mutation type over the other. This supports a divergence from 103 equal rates that would be expected under polymerase errors alone, and therefore supports 104 the action of one or mutagens. (D) Comparison of contextual patterns between A>T and T>A 105 mutations in tree rescaled mutational spectra. Each point shows the same mutational context 106 in each mutation type, for example A[A>T]C and A[T>A]C. Points show median values across 107 the eight hantaviruses with at least 160 A>T mutations and at least 160 T>A mutations; this 108 filtering is applied to ensure there are sufficient mutations to compare contexts [22]. The 109 significant positive correlation between non-symmetric contexts supports the action of one or 110 more mutagens that causes A>T and T>A mutations with the same surrounding context 111 preferences. 112 113 We next tested for the impact of mutagens by comparing the relative rates of symmetric 114 mutation types [22] and found evidence of mutagens causing G>T (median 2.6-fold elevation), 115 G>A (median 1.3-fold elevation), A>G (median 1.3-fold elevation) and T>G (median 1.6-fold 116 elevation) mutations (permutation test P < 0.05, Figure 1). We previously found evidence of 117 mutagens causing G>T, A>G and T>G mutations in influenza A virus [22], which indicates 118 either common mutagen exposures between the viruses or exposure to distinct sets of 119 mutagens that induce similar mutational patterns. Conversely, we did not find evidence of a 120 mutagen causing G>A mutations in influenza A virus [22], which indicates that hantaviruses 121 are exposed to at least one mutagen that does not influence influenza A virus. 122 123 As T>A and A>T mutations occur at roughly equal rates after tree rescaling (Figure 1, Figure 124 S2), their elevation relative to SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus may be due to either the 125 hantavirus polymerase making more errors between A and T nucleotides, and/or elevated 126 exposure to mutagens that cause A>T and T>A mutations. To distinguish between these 127 possibilities, we examined the contextual preferences within these mutation types. If 128 polymerase errors are responsible, A>T and T>A would exhibit symmetric contextual 129 preferences [19, 22]. However, we observe only a weak correlation between symmetric 130 contexts (Figure S3). Conversely, we observe a strong correlation between the same contexts 131 in A>T and T>A mutations (for example, A[A>T]C and A[T>A]C; Pearson’s R = 0.93, 132 randomisation P < 0.001; Figure 1). Both mutations typically occur most frequently in CXG 133 contexts (where X represents the mutated base) and occur very rarely in XT contexts (Figure 134 S4). This strongly supports exposure to one or more mutagens that introduce A>T and T>A 135 mutations at similar rates with the same contextual preferences. This further suggests that the 136 elevation of A>T and T>A mutations in hantaviruses compared with influenza A virus and 137 SARS-CoV-2 is due to mutagen exposure rather than polymerase errors. 138 139 Drivers of differences in mutational patterns across hantaviruses 140 We next examined drivers of variation in mutational patterns between hantaviruses. We 141 initially tested for an impact of viral evolutionary history and found no evidence that the 142 proportion of any mutation type follows the hantavirus phylogenetic tree (continuous 143 association index P > 0.05 in each case; Figure 2). This indicates that viral genetic factors 144 have limited direct impact on the mutational spectrum and therefore suggests that variation 145 between viruses predominantly arises from extrinsic factors. 146 147 148 Figure 2. Variation in mutational spectrum across hantaviruses. (A) The cladogram 149 shows the phylogenetic relationships between the 14 analysed hantaviruses [2]. Mutation 150 types are shown as proportions within the respective spectrum and proportions are normalised 151 so each column runs from zero to one. (B) Principal component analysis of seven hantaviruses 152 with known human disease associations (Table S1) based on mutation type proportions. 153 Viruses do not cluster by associated human disease. (C) The proportion of G>T mutations 154 within the tree rescaled spectrum is shown for each hantavirus. 155 156 We further found no evidence that differences in mutational spectra are associated with host 157 order or host family (ANOVA P > 0.05, Figure S5), or that any mutation type follows the host 158 phylogeny (continuous association index P > 0.05, Table S2). This suggests that the 159 hantavirus mutational spectrum is not greatly influenced by host factors that are conserved at 160 the level of host family or host order. 161 162 We next tested whether there is evidence of differential mutational spectra between 163 hantaviruses associated with distinct disease in humans. We found no separation of viruses 164 associated with HFRS from those associated with HPS when clustering based on mutational 165 patterns and observed no mutation types that differ by associated disease (ANOVA P > 0.05; 166 Figures 2, S6). This suggests that differences in human disease between viruses are not 167 driven by alternative tissue tropism within the reservoir species. 168 169 We next examined variation in the level of G>T mutations across hantaviruses, which we have 170 previously found can be associated with replication sites in RNA viruses and bacteria [18, 19]. 171 We found that the level of G>T mutations varies markedly between hantaviruses, from 1.8% 172 of mutational burden (accounting for genomic composition) in Khabarovsk virus to 9.5% in 173 Thailand virus (Figure 2). This variation may be driven by differential replication site 174 preferences in different viruses and/or by distinct mutagen levels across host species. In 175 potential support of the latter scenario, Seoul virus exhibits lower G>T mutations than the other 176 murinae-associated hantaviruses (Figure 2). Previous work has found a lower rate of somatic 177 G>T mutations in gastrointestinal tissue of Rattus norvegicus (a major natural host of Seoul 178 virus [2]) compared to Mus musculus [28]. This may suggest that mutagens produced by the 179 host can impact the genetic material of both host and virus and further indicate that variation 180 in G>T level across hantaviruses is influenced by the level of one or more mutagens produced 181 by the host. 182 183 Impact of host antiviral proteins on hantavirus mutagenesis 184 We next examined whether host antiviral proteins may impact hantavirus mutational patterns. 185 We initially developed a “ZAP enrichment score” that calculates the relative ZAP activity by 186 comparing contexts impacted by ZAP with those not impacted by ZAP (see Methods). This 187 score is applied to each mutation type within the tree rescaled mutational spectrum of each 188 virus and examines evidence for ZAP activity through the magnitude of the enrichment (for 189 mutation types that remove ZAP contexts) or suppression (for mutation types that introduce 190 ZAP contexts) of ZAP-associated contexts. 191 192 We observe consistent evidence of ZAP-mediated selection in C>T, T>C and A>G mutations 193 (permutation test P < 0.05; Figures 1, 3). However, we do not observe evidence of reduction 194 of ZAP-associated mutations in T>G mutations, similar to influenza A virus [22]. This indicates 195 that ZAP-mediated selection predominantly acts upon high frequency transition mutations. 196 Alternatively, as T>G is caused by at least one mutagen (Figure 1), ZAP-mediated selection 197 may be outweighed by this mutagen. While several hantaviruses exhibit an elevation of G>A 198 mutations in ZAP-associated contexts, we do not observe a consistent elevation (Figure 3). 199 In particular, Cao Bang virus is an outlier within G>A mutations and does not contain any 200 sampled G>A mutations in ZAP-associated contexts (Figure S7), despite 190 sampled G>A 201 mutations. Cao Bang virus is not an outlier for other mutation types, suggesting that this is not 202 due to reduced ZAP-mediated selection. We find a significant correlation between the 203 magnitude of ZAP enrichment in G>A mutations and the C>T/G>A symmetric mutation type 204 ratio (permutation test P < 0.05 including and excluding Cao Bang virus; Figure S8). This may 205 indicate that hantaviruses with reduced ZAP enrichment in G>A mutations are more exposed 206 to an additional mutagen driving G>A mutations under different contextual preferences, which 207 reduces the overall enrichment of ZAP-associated contexts. 208 209 210 Figure 3. Influence of host ZAP and APOBEC family proteins on hantavirus 211 mutagenesis. (A) We developed a ZAP enrichment score that calculates relative ZAP activity 212 through the enrichment (for mutation types that remove ZAP contexts) or suppression (for 213 mutation types that introduce ZAP contexts) of ZAP-associated contexts. This score was 214 calculated for each mutation type in each virus that contains at least 160 mutations within the 215 respective mutation type (see Methods). The distributions of these scores are shown for each 216 mutation type. T>A and A>T mutations are not included as they do not introduce or remove 217 ZAP contexts. C>A, C>G, G>C, G>T and A>C are not shown as they contain a maximum of 218 two viruses with at least 160 mutations. (B) The proportion of C>T mutations with each 219 upstream nucleotide in tree rescaled spectra. * shows permutation test P < 0.05 comparing 220 the distributions of T[C>T] mutations with those of the other upstream nucleotides. 221 222 We do not find evidence that any hantavirus exhibits consistently higher ZAP activity across 223 mutation types, or of consistent elevation of ZAP activity within a host family (Figure 2). full_text_sections.full_text: Hantavirus mutagenesis is impacted by mutagens and host antiviral proteins 1 Christopher Ruis1,2,3,4*, Julian Parkhill2, R. Andres Floto1,3,5 2 3 Affiliations 4 1Victor Phillip Dahdaleh Heart and Lung Research Institute, Department of Medicine, 5 University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 6 2Department of Veterinary Medicine, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 7 3Cambridge Centre for AI in Medicine, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 8 4Biological and Chemical Research Centre, University of Warsaw, Warsaw, Poland 9 5Department of Medicine, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK 10 *Correspondence to: Christopher Ruis (cr628@cam.ac.uk) 11 Abstract 12 Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that infect humans with high fatality rates. We 13 currently have a poor understanding of the processes that contribute to hantavirus 14 mutagenesis and therefore the potential for viral adaptation. To understand the drivers of 15 mutations in hantaviruses, we calculated and compared mutational spectra across 14 16 divergent hantavirus species. We found that mutagens that are conserved across host species 17 have a major impact on hantaviruses mutagenesis, contributing to at least six of the 12 18 possible mutation types. We found differences in mutational signatures across hantaviruses, 19 some of which may be due to variation in host mutagen levels that are known to influence 20 somatic mutations. However, we could find no evidence for differential mutational signatures 21 between viruses associated with distinct diseases in humans and no evidence of tissue 22 tropism differences between reservoir hosts. Using a novel method to quantify the impact of 23 ZAP-mediated selection, we found that ZAP greatly influences mutational patterns in transition 24 mutation types across hantaviruses. We also find evidence that APOBEC family proteins drive 25 mutagenesis in all hantaviruses, with the likely exception of Nova virus. Our results therefore 26 provide strong support that mutagens and host antiviral proteins are major contributors to 27 hantavirus mutagenesis, thereby generating the genetic diversity necessary for viral 28 adaptation. 29 Introduction 30 Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that naturally infect hosts within the orders 31 Rodentia, Eulipotyphla and Chiroptera [1–3]. Each hantavirus typically exhibits a close 32 association with one or a small number of host species within which it establishes 33 predominantly asymptomatic infections [3]. For example, Hantaan virus lives within the striped 34 field mouse (Apodemus agrarius), while Andes virus is carried by the long-tailed pygmy rice 35 rat (Oligozomys longicaudatus) [2, 4]. This host association results in most hantaviruses 36 exhibiting strong geographical restriction, determined by the range of their host [1, 3]. The 37 exception is Seoul virus which infects black rats (Rattus rattus) and brown rats (Rattus 38 norvegicus) and correspondingly exhibits a global distribution concomitant with that of its hosts 39 [2]. 40 41 Hantaviruses are capable of infecting multiple cell types, including endothelial cells, epithelial 42 cells, macrophages, follicular dendritic cells and lymphocytes and can be detected in multiple 43 tissues within their reservoir hosts including the lungs and kidneys [3, 5]. Within humans, 44 hantaviruses can cause two distinct diseases, which are associated with different viruses and 45 therefore geographical regions [1, 3, 6, 7]. Human hantavirus cases in Eurasia are associated 46 with Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), while those in the Americas are 47 associated with Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS; also called Hantavirus 48 Cardiopulmonary Syndrome or HCPS) [6, 7]. 49 50 Human hantavirus infections predominantly occur through inhalation of secretions from the 51 major host species, including faeces, saliva and urine [6, 7]. More rarely, infections can occur 52 through bites [6]. Andes virus is currently the only hantavirus with documented human-to- 53 human transmission; such events are associated with close contact and can lead to small 54 clusters of cases [8, 9]. However, zoonotic transmission events are frequent enough to lead 55 to an estimated 10,000 to 100,000 human hantavirus cases each year with an estimated 56 fatality rate of <1% to 40% depending on the virus and outbreak [6]. 57 58 Hantaviruses are within the genus Orthohantavirus and the Bunyaviridae family and as such 59 have a negative sense single stranded RNA genome [10, 11]. The genome is organised into 60 three segments, termed large (L), medium (M) and small (S), of which the M segment encodes 61 the viral glycoproteins Gn and Gc [10]. The substitution rate of hantaviruses is estimated to be 62 in the range of 10-4 to 10-2 substitutions/site/year, typical of RNA viruses [12]. This high 63 substitution rate suggests that hantaviruses are capable of rapid adaptation. 64 65 Adaptation relies on the generation of diversity and therefore on mutagenesis. To understand 66 microbial adaptation, we therefore need an understanding of the mutational processes that 67 contribute to mutagenesis. However, we currently have a poor understanding of these factors 68 within hantaviruses and therefore the processes that may assist or constrain hantavirus 69 adaptation. We and others have recently demonstrated that mutational signatures (context- 70 specific patterns of nucleotide substitution initially applied to detect the drivers of 71 tumourigenesis [13–16]) can identify active mutational processes in microbes [17–26]. We 72 have applied these methods to identify both intrinsic mutational processes encoded by the 73 microbe and extrinsic lifestyle-associated mutagen exposures [18–20, 22]. In this study, we 74 examine and compare mutational patterns across hantaviruses to identify mutational 75 processes that may contribute to hantavirus adaptation. 76 Results 77 78 Mutagens impact hantavirus mutagenesis 79 We calculated single base substitution (SBS) mutational spectra for 14 hantavirus species that 80 exhibit at least 600 sampled mutations [27] amongst M segment genetic sequences (Figure 81 1, Table S1, see Methods). We additionally carried out “tree rescaling” of each spectrum by 82 sequence composition across the respective phylogenetic tree [22]. The overall mutational 83 spectrum is highly similar across viruses at the overall level (median cosine similarity 0.978; 84 Figure S1), supporting conservation of most mutational processes. We found that, as 85 expected, each spectrum is dominated by transition mutations (median 76.7% unscaled, 86 78.1% tree rescaled; Figures 1, S2). In contrast to SARS-CoV-2 [19, 26] and influenza A virus 87 [22], T>A and A>T are typically the most common transversion mutations by raw count (Figure 88 S2). However, following tree rescaling, G>T mutations occur at a similar rate to T>A and A>T 89 mutations (Figure S2). 90 91 92 Figure 1. Mutagens influence hantavirus mutagenesis. (A) Cladogram of the evolutionary 93 relationships between the 14 analysed hantaviruses. The heatmap shows the respective host 94 family, host order, associated human disease (where known) and geographical distribution of 95 each virus. Tip labels include the virus name and, in parentheses, the common English name 96 and scientific name of the respective predominant host species. (B) The SBS mutational 97 spectrum of Seoul virus is shown as proportions of raw mutation counts (left hand panel) and 98 as the proportion of mutations within the tree rescaled spectrum (right hand panel). Asterisks 99 in the right hand panel show C>T and G>A mutations that remove ZAP-associated CG 100 contexts. (C) Comparison of symmetric mutation types in tree rescaled mutational spectra. * 101 shows randomisation P < 0.05, supporting a significant difference from a ratio of one and 102 therefore an elevation of one mutation type over the other. analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses that infect humans with high fatality rates, and the processes driving their mutagenesis are poorly understood.
analysis.methods: The authors calculated and compared single‑base substitution mutational spectra across 14 divergent hantavirus species using M‑segment sequences that contained at least 600 sampled mutations (A3).
analysis.results: Mutagens conserved across host species contribute to at least six of the twelve possible mutation types (A4); mutational signatures differ among hantaviruses, possibly reflecting host mutagen level variation (A5); no signature differences were found between viruses linked to distinct human diseases or host tissue tropism (A6); ZAP strongly influences transition‑type mutations (A7); and APOBEC family proteins drive mutagenesis in all hantaviruses except likely Nova virus (A8).
analysis.contribution: The findings support that host‑derived mutagens and antiviral proteins are major contributors to hantavirus mutagenesis, generating genetic diversity that may facilitate viral adaptation (A9).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic viruses with high fatality rates and limited knowledge of mutagenic processes. Methods: Researchers compared single‑base substitution spectra across 14 hantavirus species using M‑segment sequences with ≥600 mutations (A3). Results: Conserved host mutagens affect at least six of twelve mutation types (A4); mutational signatures vary among viruses, possibly due to host mutagen levels (A5); no differences were seen between viruses causing different human diseases or tissue tropisms (A6); ZAP influences transition mutations (A7); APOBEC proteins drive mutagenesis in all but likely Nova virus (A8). Contribution: The study shows host mutagens and antiviral proteins are key drivers of hantavirus genetic diversity, informing adaptation potential (A9). Limitations: Only abstract and partial text are available; detailed methods and quantitative data are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 突变受突变原和宿主抗病毒蛋白的影响

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒是新出现的动物源病毒,能够感染人类并导致高致死率,其突变机制尚不清楚。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者计算并比较了14种不同的汉坦病毒物种的单碱基置换突变谱,使用包含至少600个采样突变的M段序列(A3)。
analysis_zh.results: 跨宿主物种保守的诱变剂贡献了至少12种可能突变类型中的六种(A4);汉坦病毒的突变特征存在差异,可能反映宿主诱变剂水平的变异(A5);在与不同人类疾病或宿主组织嗜性相关的病毒之间未发现特征差异(A6);ZAP显著影响转变型突变(A7);APOBEC家族蛋白驱动除可能的Nova病毒外所有汉坦病毒的突变(A8)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究结果支持宿主来源的诱变剂和抗病毒蛋白是汉坦病毒突变的主要因素,产生的遗传多样性可能促进病毒适应(A9)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要和部分文本;未报告详细的实验步骤、样本来源及定量效应大小。

papers.title: Characteristics and Superspreading Potential of Andes Virus Person-to-Person Transmission.
papers.abstract: By using historical contact tracing data, we estimated that 23.4% of case-patients caused 80% of Andes virus (ANDV) person-to-person transmission. We demonstrated a low but nonnegligible probability of observing a large-scale ANDV infection outbreak in a rodent-free setting consisting of close contacts, despite the historically self-limited person-to-person transmission of ANDV.
